data.title: Trenčianske Teplice – Čertova skala, a hillfort on the road to Moravia
data.excerpt: On a rocky hill above Trenčianske Teplice, on the border between the Celtic occupation of the territory of present-day Slovakia and the mixed Celtic-Lusatian Púchov culture, the Celts built a small hillfort of only 0.18 ha. The Suebi later used it briefly as a refuge, and in the 9th–11th centuries the Slavs turned it into an important guard hillfort with a smithy; a Celtic sacrificial site lay close by.
data.metaTitle: Čertova skala – a hillfort above Trenčianske Teplice
data.metaDescription: Čertova skala above Trenčianske Teplice: a small Celtic hillfort of 0.18 ha, later a refuge of the Suebi and a Slavic guard hillfort of the 9th century.

keyFacts.label: Area of the hillfort
keyFacts.value: 75 × 25 metres, approximately 0.18 ha – in terms of area the hillfort is one of the small fortifications.

keyFacts.label: Origin of the name
keyFacts.value: The hillfort is named after a hole in the rock at the very top of the hill; the devil is said to have stamped into the rock here in order to hide his treasure, and his footprint remained behind.

keyFacts.label: The view from the summit
keyFacts.value: On clear days there is a magnificent view from Čertova skala of the Strážov mountains, the White Carpathians and the surrounding villages.

keyFacts.label: Smithy / jeweller’s workshop
keyFacts.value: Evidence of a workshop was discovered on the hillfort, including semi-finished pieces, an unfinished fibula and tools such as a drill, a chisel and a cold chisel.

keyFacts.label: Celtic sacrificial site
keyFacts.value: An important Celtic cult place with a large quantity of burnt metal objects, glass, bones and pottery was discovered in the vicinity of the hillfort.

keyFacts.label: Spurs from Pobedim
keyFacts.value: The three spurs that were found belong to the type made at the hillfort in Pobedim, dated to the first third of the 9th century.

keyFacts.label: Axe-shaped currency bars
keyFacts.value: The finds from the period of the Principality of Nitra and Great Moravia also include axe-shaped currency bars – the Slavic currency of the time.

timeline.description: On the border between Celtic occupation and the Celtic-Lusatian Púchov culture, the Celts built an important hillfort at the site of Čertova skala.

timeline.description: After the demise of the Celtic occupation the site was temporarily inhabited by Germanic peoples – in the Migration Period the hillfort was briefly occupied as a refuge by the Germanic Suebi.

timeline.description: The Slavs who settled in the Teplička valley made use of the abandoned Celtic hillfort and built an important guard hillfort here, probably inhabited by craftsmen as well.

children.text: The area around Trenčín played a specific role in the history of Slovakia, conditioned above all by its geographical setting. It lies on the boundary between the mountainous and the lowland parts of the Carpathian arc, where the oldest human cultures arose and developed in the course of history. This area is connected above all with the road leading across the White Carpathians towards Moravia and into the territory of Bohemia. In the Late Iron Age – that is, in the La Tène period – it was precisely in this area that the border ran between the Celtic occupation of the territory of present-day Slovakia and the mixed Celtic-Lusatian Púchov culture. On the border between these two similar cultures the Celts built an important hillfort, which today lies in the cadastral area of Trenčianske Teplice, at a site with the telling name Čertova skala (Devil’s Rock).

Čertova skala is a rocky hill above the Oliwa holiday centre. It lies close to Trenčianske Teplice. On clear days there is a magnificent view from here of the Strážov mountains, the White Carpathians and the surrounding villages. From this spa town you can get here along the yellow waymarked trail, and access is also possible from Oliwa. You cross the brook that flows on the right-hand side from Oliwa and come onto a forest track which leads directly below the hillfort. There are several ways of getting to the top; the bolder and above all the fitter will manage it by climbing up the rocks, while those who prefer comfort will certainly find an easy path to the summit.

Čertova skala takes its name from a hole in the rock at the very top of this little hill; the devil is said to have stamped into the rock here in order to hide his treasure, and his footprint remained in the rock after him.

blocks.alt: A plan of the hillfort of Čertova skala

children.text: Within the valley of the river Teplička, occupation as early as the Bronze Age was discovered, at the locality of Čvirigovec. In the Late Iron Age, as has already been indicated, the area was occupied by the Celts (Celto-Lusatians), who built the hillfort of Čertova skala mentioned above. After the demise of the Celtic occupation the site was temporarily inhabited by Germanic peoples at the time of the Migration Period (approximately the 5th–6th centuries). Subsequently Slavic tribes moved into the territory of present-day Slovakia and gradually occupied not only the fertile lowland areas, but did not avoid the mountainous parts of the territory of present-day Slovakia either. The Slavs who settled in the Teplička valley made use of the abandoned Celtic hillfort and occupied this place again, building here in the 9th–11th centuries an important guard hillfort which was at the same time probably also inhabited by craftsmen (for example the remains of a smithy).

children.text: In terms of area the hillfort is one of the small fortifications – it measures 75 × 25 metres and covers about 0.18 ha. On the southern side of the hillfort we find a relatively well-preserved and visible rampart fortification. Remains of the fortification can be found in several other places as well, especially in the more accessible parts of the hillfort, where the natural setting did not in itself provide sufficient conditions for defence. A rampart with a ditch also divides the interior of the hillfort into an acropolis and a bailey.
The densest occupation of Čertova skala can be observed in the Middle and Late La Tène period (the Late Iron Age – the Celts,

), which left the largest number of various objects on the hillfort. The Púchov culture, or Púchov group, was an archaeological culture lasting approximately from 300 BC to AD 180 (according to some less common views as late as the 4th century AD); in the 1st century BC it extended over northern, central and western Slovakia, north-eastern Moravia and Lesser Poland, and after the turn of the era only over central (predominantly northern) Slovakia and the area around Kraków. The Púchov culture in the narrower sense begins in the middle of the 2nd century BC. Among the most interesting finds from this period are bronze brooches, parts of a necklace, various typical iron fibulae (for example of the Neuheim type), belt clasps, iron spiral pendants, a finger ring, a fragment of a scythe and of a sickle, and metal parts of a plough, which are known from other Late La Tène hillforts as well.

blocks.caption: Finds mostly from the Late Iron Age (the Púchov culture)
blocks.alt: Finds mostly from the Late Iron Age (the Púchov culture)

children.text: After the people of the Púchov culture had disappeared from it, the hillfort was briefly occupied in the Migration Period as a refuge by

This is attested, for example, by a fibula that is attributed to this Germanic tribe. Several earrings and finger rings that were found are also assigned to this period. Čertova skala, too, is evidence for the older theories which hold that at a certain period the Suebi were forced to use various older fortified sites as places of refuge.

After the departure of the Germanic peoples from the territory of present-day Slovakia we can observe on the hillfort Slavic occupation falling within the period of the Principality of Nitra and of Great Moravia, but the hillfort with its Slavic occupation survived for many decades after the fall of Great Moravia as well (the 10th–11th centuries). The focus of the occupation in the Early Middle Ages, however, we place in the 9th century, in the period of the Principality of Nitra and subsequently of Great Moravia, as is suggested by the quantity of objects found that are typical of this period, for example axe-shaped currency bars (Slavic currency), part of a bridle, three belt strap ends and three spurs. This type of spur was made at the hillfort in Pobedim and we assign it unambiguously to the period of the first third of the 9th century.

children.text: Evidence for the existence of a smithy, or rather a jeweller’s workshop, was also discovered on the hillfort. Some semi-finished pieces and an unfinished product – a fibula – have even survived. Of the tools that were evidently used in production, a drill (a spoon bit), a chisel and a cold chisel were found above all. Because the find spot had been damaged by metal detectorists, however, it was not possible to establish unambiguously whether the workshops date from the Iron Age or whether they were the workshops of our ancestors, the Slavs.
The Celtic sacrificial site „Nad Družstevnou tehelňou – Seravy“

In the vicinity of the hillfort, at the locality „Nad starou tehelňou“ – in a hilltop position, an important Celtic cult place was discovered – a sacrificial site, on which amateur searchers and later also archaeologists found a large quantity of metal objects – above all fibulae and other jewellery, glass vessels, as well as bones and other finds, especially various pottery. All these objects bore marked traces of a strong fire, into which they had been thrown for the purpose of purification rituals. It is almost certain that the cult place served precisely the inhabitants of the hillfort of Čertova skala and the adjoining Celtic settlement. A similar sacrificial site was discovered in the 1980s at Prosné.
